1086.title: Holy things without a Temple
1086.hook: the fifth order: Temple offerings and kosher slaughter
1086.carry: learning the offering counts as bringing it
1086.howItsDone: Jews who study Talmud learn the order of Kodashim even though Temple offerings are not brought today, and some traditional prayer books include passages about the offerings in the morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, warning the witnesses: one seal, and no two faces alike. Your line: a whole world. Today, a new week, and a builder's notebook.

One tractate of the Mishnah reads like a builder's notebook. Gates and their names. Chambers and what each was for. Courtyards, steps, the size of the altar, the places where priests kept watch at night. It's called Middot, measurements. It belongs to the fifth of the Mishnah's six orders, beside tractates on animal offerings, grain offerings, birds, firstborn animals, and what happens when someone uses holy property for themselves. No Temple stands today, and nobody brings these offerings. Yet students still open these pages.
screen: `A BUILDER'S NOTEBOOK: MIDDOT.` → `OFFERINGS, FIRSTBORN, BIRDS.` → `NO TEMPLE, STILL STUDIED.`

segments.voice: Kodashim. Holy things. In the Mishnah, holiness works like a status. An animal, a measure of flour, a coin: once it's dedicated to the Temple, it is set apart. It doesn't look different. It is different. Three turns on that idea. First, misuse. A whole tractate, Me'ilah, deals with someone who takes a holy thing and uses it as ordinary property. That's the danger: not dirt, but treating the set-apart as just another thing. Second, rhythm. The tractate Tamid describes the daily offering, morning and evening, the Temple's steady heartbeat. One opinion in the Talmud says the daily prayers were set to match those offerings. So a Jew praying the morning and afternoon services today is keeping time with a Temple clock. Third, study. With no Temple, what do you do with all these laws? The Talmud, in the tractate Menachot, answers: whoever studies the law of an offering is counted as if they had brought it. The prophet Hosea had already pictured words offered in place of bulls. So the pages became the altar. People learn the measurements of a building they've never seen, the way you might remember the layout of a grandparent's house. And tucked between the offerings is one more surprise, a tractate about ordinary meat. That's tomorrow. For today: something becomes holy when it's set apart, and stays holy as long as it's treated that way.

Hold one in mind, and ask the question of Me'ilah: when have I treated it as ordinary? No verdict; just notice where the line is.

1087.title: Everyday holiness (Chullin)
1087.hook: the tractate on ordinary meat sits in the order of holy things
1087.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher follow the laws of slaughter and of separating meat and milk developed from tractate Chullin; others keep some of these customs or none, and some Jewish homes treat the Shabbat table as a place of blessing and welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kodashim: holiness as a status, something set apart. Your line: holy things. Today, the ordinary meat filed among them.

Chullin. The word means ordinary things: not dedicated, not for the altar. Just food. The chicken for a Friday night dinner, the beef in a weekday stew. A whole tractate of the Mishnah covers it: how an animal is slaughtered for eating at home, which creatures may be eaten, how meat and milk are kept apart. And here's the odd part. The Mishnah doesn't file it with the blessings over food. It puts it right in the middle of the order of holy things, beside the Temple's offerings.
screen: `CHULLIN: ORDINARY THINGS.` → `THE WEEKDAY STEW.` → `FILED AMONG THE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Everyday holiness. Start with the placement. The Mishnah could have filed ordinary meat anywhere. It set it down among the offerings. One way to read that: the care given to the altar now follows the food home. The same attention, the same rules about how an animal dies, apply at a kitchen table. Second, the kitchen itself. The Torah's line is short, in the old JPS translation: "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk." From that line, which the Torah gives more than once, the Mishnah and the Talmud build the separation of meat and milk, a chapter of Chullin and much more after it. Third, the ending. The last chapter of Chullin is about a bird's nest. Deuteronomy says that if you come upon a nest with the mother sitting on the young or the eggs, you let the mother go before you take them. So the tractate on everyday meat ends with an animal mother, and a law that asks for restraint at the moment you could take everything. The Mishnah's closing lines reason from it: if a light commandment like this carries the promise of a long life, how much more the weighty ones. Fourth, the table. With the Temple gone, a teaching in the Talmud says, a person's table atones for them, the way the altar once did. So the order of holy things makes a quiet claim. Holiness isn't only in the sanctuary. It's in how you slaughter, how you cook, what you leave, and who you feed.

1088.title: Purities
1088.hook: the sixth order: ritual purity, which is a state, not a moral grade
1088.howItsDone: Purity laws tied to the Temple are studied rather than practiced today; Jews who keep halacha wash hands ritually before bread and on waking, and keep the laws of the mikveh and family purity that come from this order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chullin: ordinary meat, filed among holy things, ending with the mother bird. Your line: everyday holiness. Today, some men who asked not to be left out.

A small group of men come to Moses with a complaint. Passover is here, and they can't keep it. They've been near a dead body, so they're ritually impure. They aren't asking forgiveness. They ask, in effect, why should we be kept back? They had done nothing wrong. Someone had died, and someone had to tend the dead. Moses doesn't know the answer. He asks God, and the answer in the book of Numbers is a second date for Passover, for anyone who was impure or far away.
screen: `WHY SHOULD WE BE KEPT BACK?` → `THEY HAD TENDED THE DEAD.` → `A SECOND PASSOVER.`

segments.voice: Tohorot. Purities. The last of the Mishnah's six orders, and it turns on a Hebrew pair, taharah and tumah: ritual purity and ritual impurity. First, where impurity comes from. In the Torah: from death, from certain dead creatures, from some skin conditions, from giving birth, and from the body's own flows. Birth, death, the body. None of these is a crime. They're life. Second, what impurity does. It mattered for one thing above all: contact with the holy. A person in a state of impurity didn't enter the sanctuary or eat holy food until it passed. The men in Numbers weren't punished. They were paused. Third, how it ends. Again and again the Torah's answer is water and time: bathe, and wait until evening. No confession, no fine. A change of state. Fourth, the machinery. The order opens with a long tractate called Kelim, vessels, on which objects can carry impurity, and it begins by naming fathers of impurity. Fathers again, like the fathers of work and of damage; the rabbis like a family tree for their categories. With no Temple, much of this order isn't lived day to day. But pieces are: a tractate called Yadayim, hands, stands behind washing hands before bread, and tomorrow's subject comes from here too. Pure and impure here are not good and bad. They're more like awake and asleep: states a body passes through, with a way back.

segments.voice: Think of something you missed through no fault of your own: a celebration skipped while caring for someone sick, a holiday spent in a hospital corridor, a plan dropped because you were far from home. 1089.title: The mikveh
1089.hook: a pool of natural water for ritual immersion
1089.howItsDone: In traditional practice, people converting to Judaism immerse in a mikveh, and some brides, married women, men before holy days, and new dishes are immersed too; Jewish communities differ on which of these they keep, and some have created new immersion customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tohorot: impurity is a state, and water and time bring you back. Your line: a state, not a grade. Today, the water itself.

In the first chapter of Genesis, the waters are gathered into one place and dry land appears. Then God names them, in the old JPS translation: "the gathering together of the waters called He Seas." The Hebrew behind that gathering is mikveh. The same word names something much smaller today: a pool, often in a quiet building with a discreet door, where a person walks down a few steps into water, goes under, and comes back up.
screen: `THE GATHERING OF THE WATERS.` → `A SMALL POOL, A QUIET DOOR.` → `DOWN THE STEPS, UNDER, UP.`

segments.voice: Mikveh. A gathering of water. First, what kind of water. A mikveh isn't filled from a tap like a bathtub. The Mishnah's tractate Mikvaot insists the water be gathered the way the world gathers it: rain, or a spring, not carried in by hand in buckets. Second, a ladder. The tractate opens by ranking gatherings of water, from a shallow puddle upward, each fit for more than the one below. At the top: mayim chayim, living waters, water that flows from its source. The Torah uses that phrase in its purity laws, and the rabbis hear in it water that is alive, still moving. Third, who goes in. In traditional practice, a person becoming a Jew immerses in a mikveh. So do brides before their wedding. Some men go before Shabbat or Yom Kippur. New dishes can be dipped too. And married women who keep the laws of family purity immerse monthly, which is tomorrow's subject. Fourth, a play on words from Rabbi Akiva. The prophet Jeremiah calls God, in the old JPS translation, "O LORD, the hope of Israel." In Hebrew, hope there is mikveh. So, says Rabbi Akiva in the Mishnah, God is the mikveh of Israel: just as a mikveh makes the impure pure, so God makes Israel pure. The pool in the basement and the hope of a nation share a word.
screen: `GATHERED BY RAIN OR SPRING, NOT BUCKETS.` · `A LADDER OF WATERS.` · `WHO GOES DOWN THE STEPS.` · `AKIVA: GOD, THE MIKVEH OF ISRAEL.` · then, large: `LIVING WATERS.`

segments.voice: Fill a bowl or a sink, or hold your hands under a gently running tap, and lower them a little at a time, feeling the water climb past your knuckles and wrists. At a mikveh, nothing is meant to come between the water and the skin, so let it touch everything. Then lift your hands out, let them drip, and notice the difference between before and after.
Mikveh. A gathering of water: a pool of rain or spring water for immersion, and in Jeremiah, a word for hope. Today's word.

1090.title: Family purity
1090.hook: many observant couples keep laws of separation and immersion; it is a private practice
1090.howItsDone: Orthodox couples keep the laws of family purity as binding, with the wife immersing in a mikveh before they resume intimacy; some Jews in other movements keep adapted forms, others do not, and mikveh visits are kept discreet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mikveh: gathered rain and spring water, and the hope of Israel. Your line: living waters. Today, a practice meant to stay unseen.

Some practices are meant to be seen: a sukkah in the yard, a menorah in the window. This one is meant not to be. A married woman, after a stretch of days apart from her husband, goes down the steps of a mikveh, under the water, and back up. Then the two of them come back together. Her neighbors don't need to know she went. Jewish law calls this family purity, and couples who keep it keep it quietly.
screen: `A SUKKAH IN THE YARD.` → `A MENORAH IN THE WINDOW.` → `THIS ONE, UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Family purity. In Hebrew, taharat hamishpacha. First, the source. Leviticus describes a woman's monthly flow as a time of ritual impurity, and says a husband and wife don't come together during it. The Mishnah gives these laws a whole tractate, Niddah, inside the order of purities you met two days ago. Second, the rhythm. Couples who keep these laws step back from physical closeness during the woman's period and for a time of counting afterward that the rabbis set. Then she immerses in a mikveh, and they come together again. Apart, then together, month after month. Third, a reason. The Talmud asks why the Torah set this up, and Rabbi Meir answers: so that she will be as dear to her husband as on the day she stood under the wedding canopy. That's one voice. Some who keep these laws say they keep them first because they are commanded, and find their meaning from inside the practice. Fourth, what it isn't. Remember: a state, not a grade. Ritual impurity here says nothing about a woman being dirty or less. It's a status tied to the body's own rhythm, and it ends with water and time. Jews hold these laws in different ways. Orthodox communities teach them as binding law. Some in other movements keep them in adapted forms, and some don't keep them. For those who do, one thing is shared: it belongs to the couple. Mikveh visits are kept discreet, and nobody is expected to explain.

1091.title: Reading a mishnah
1091.hook: a case, a few opinions, and often an anonymous ruling
1091.howItsDone: Jews who study Mishnah sometimes learn it with a partner or in a class, reading each mishnah aloud, naming its case and its voices, and some study a set amount each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, family purity: apart, then together, kept quietly by the couples who keep it. Your line: a private practice. Today, back to the Talmud's very first question.

From what time may the Shema be recited in the evening? That's the question that opens the tractate Berakhot. Not why. Not whether. When. And the answer doesn't come in one voice. It comes as a small crowd: Rabbi Eliezer, then the Sages, then Rabban Gamliel. And then, as if the page can't help itself, a story about Rabban Gamliel's sons coming home late from a wedding. You met this mishnah back in year one. Now, with the six orders behind you, here's how to read it.
screen: `FROM WHAT TIME?` → `A SMALL CROWD OF VOICES.` → `SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: Reading a mishnah. Four moves. First, the case. A mishnah tends to start with a concrete question, and this one answers with a picture, not a clock: from the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion. Those are priests who were impure, who immersed, and who waited for evening. Water and time, from the last few days, become the start of the evening prayer. Second, the voices. Until when? Rabbi Eliezer says, until the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say, until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says, until dawn rises. Three answers, each with a name, and the Mishnah keeps all three. Third, the story. Rabban Gamliel's sons come home from a wedding feast and tell him they haven't said the Shema. He tells them: if dawn hasn't risen, you are still obliged to say it. Then the Mishnah explains the Sages' midnight: they set it as a fence, to keep people far from missing it. So the stricter voice turns out to be a guardrail, not a different law. Fourth, the voice with no name. Here no one argues over the start; the debate is only about the end. In other mishnahs a ruling is given with no name at all. A line like that is called stam, plain. The Talmud has a saying that an unnamed mishnah is Rabbi Meir's, and readers learn to listen hard for that plain voice. So: find the case, hear each voice by name, watch for a story, then listen for who speaks without a name.
screen: `THE CASE: FROM THE PRIESTS' MEAL.` · `THE VOICES: WATCH, MIDNIGHT, DAWN.` · `THE STORY, AND A FENCE.` · `STAM: THE VOICE WITH NO NAME.` · then, large: `A CASE, THEN VOICES.`

segments.voice: Take the mishnah you just heard and say its question to yourself: from what time, until what time? Let each voice speak in turn, Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages, Rabban Gamliel, and picture the sons at the door, late and a little worried. Notice which voice you lean toward, and that the page never makes you choose.
Reading a mishnah. A case, a few named voices, sometimes a story, and a plain voice with no name, all kept on one page. Today's word.

1092.title: The Gemara
1092.hook: the discussion of each mishnah, mostly in Aramaic
1092.howItsDone: In a study hall, students learn the Gemara aloud, with a study partner or in a class, reading the Aramaic and talking it through question by question. Daily study cycles move through it page by page.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading a mishnah: a case, named voices, and a plain voice with no name. Your line: a case, then voices. Today, what happens after the voices stop.

Yesterday's mishnah gave its answer, the hour the priests go in to eat their holy food, then a few named opinions about when the time runs out, and stopped. Neat. Short. Done. Except the page isn't done. Right underneath, in a different language, someone raises a hand. Wait. Why does the mishnah ask from when, as if we already know there's a duty at all? Where is the teacher standing when he asks that?
screen: `FROM WHEN, IN THE EVENING?` → `A NEAT ANSWER.` → `A HAND GOES UP.`

segments.voice: Gemara. The long discussion that follows each mishnah in the Talmud. The Mishnah is mostly Hebrew and mostly brief. The Gemara is mostly Aramaic, the everyday language of the sages who came after, and it is anything but brief. First, it questions the mishnah's wording. In tractate Berakhot, the Gemara asks where the mishnah's teacher is standing, and answers: on a verse. The Shema itself says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up. So the duty comes from the Torah, and the mishnah only asks when. Second, the questions keep coming. An answer is never the end of the line; it becomes the ground the next question stands on. Fine, but why start with evening and not morning? That one waits for tomorrow. Third, notice how it talks. The Gemara is full of little Aramaic signposts. Ta shema: come and hear, which means here comes a source. Mai ka mashma lan: what is it teaching us? Each one tells you what move is being made, like stage directions in a play. Fourth, notice who's in the room. Sages from different places and generations appear on one page as if they were talking across a table. The editors placed them there, so a student reading alone is never really alone. Not a list of answers, but a record of people working toward them.
screen: `IT QUESTIONS THE WORDING.` · `ONE QUESTION OPENS THE NEXT.` · `ARAMAIC SIGNPOSTS: COME AND HEAR.` · `SAGES ACROSS ONE TABLE.` · then, large: `THE CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Take one Aramaic phrase, ta shema: ta, come, and shema, hear. On the breath in, come; on the breath out, hear. If thoughts arrive, let each one be a voice joining the table, and come back to the two words.
Gemara. The discussion of each mishnah in the Talmud, mostly in Aramaic, that questions, answers and questions again. Today's word.
